draft.title: Purposes of sanctions
card: Deterrence discourages crime through fear of a sanction. Specific deterrence aims at the offender, and general deterrence aims at others who might offend.
Punishment makes the offender face a just penalty for the wrong, in proportion to how serious the crime was. Denunciation is the court publicly stating that the conduct is wrong.

Rehabilitation helps the offender change, for example through treatment or training, so they do not reoffend. Protection keeps the community safe from the offender, for example by keeping them in prison.

Section 5(1) of the Sentencing Act 1991 (Vic) sets out these five purposes. A sentence can serve several at once, and they can pull against each other. The judge weighs them to reach a fitting sentence.
draft.remember: Judges balance five purposes: rehabilitate, punish, deter, denounce and protect.

a.q: A court orders an offender to complete a drug treatment program so they can change their behaviour and stop reoffending. Which purpose does this mainly serve?
a.why: Treatment aims to change the offender so they do not reoffend, which is rehabilitation. Protection is the tempting wrong answer, but it keeps the community safe from the offender, not by changing the person.
a.clue: Which purpose is about changing the offender?

b.q: A judge imposes a long prison term on a fraudster and says it should warn other people tempted to commit similar frauds. Which purpose is the judge relying on?
b.why: The warning is aimed at other people who might offend, which is general deterrence. Specific deterrence is the tempting wrong answer, but it aims to discourage this offender, not the wider public.
b.clue: Who is the warning meant for: the offender or others?
